topics.title: Arrays
topics.description: Learn array basics, indexing, traversal and common operations.

sections.heading: What is an Array?
sections.content: An array is a collection of elements stored in an ordered sequence. In most programming languages, array elements are accessed using an index.

sections.heading: Indexing
sections.content: Array indexing usually starts from 0. For an array of n elements, the first element is at index 0 and the last element is at index n-1.

sections.heading: Traversal
sections.content: Traversal means visiting each element of an array, usually using a loop.

sections.heading: Common Operations
sections.content: Common array operations include accessing, updating, searching, inserting and deleting elements. Accessing an element by index is generally O(1).

examples.title: Finding the Largest Element
examples.explanation: Start with the first element as the maximum and compare every remaining element with it. Update the maximum whenever a larger value is found.

examples.title: Array Traversal
examples.explanation: Use a loop from index 0 to the last index to visit every element exactly once.

practice.question: What is the index of the first element in a zero-indexed array?
practice.explanation: In a zero-indexed array, the first element is stored at index 0.

practice.question: What is the index of the last element of an array containing 10 elements?
practice.explanation: For n elements in a zero-indexed array, the last index is n-1. Therefore, 10-1 = 9.

practice.question: What is the typical time complexity of accessing an array element by index?
practice.explanation: An array provides direct access to an element using its index, so access is typically O(1).

practice.question: Which operation visits every element of an array?
practice.explanation: Traversal means visiting the elements of a data structure one by one.

practice.question: What is the sum of the elements [2, 4, 6, 8]?
Which loop is commonly used to traverse an array using its index?
practice.explanation: A for loop is commonly used when the array index needs to be controlled during traversal.

practice.question: What is the largest value in [12, 7, 19, 4, 15]?
practice.explanation: Comparing all elements shows that 19 is the largest value.

practice.question: If an array has 5 elements, how many valid zero-based indices does it have?
practice.explanation: The valid indices are 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, giving a total of 5 indices.

topics.title: Linked Lists
topics.description: Understand nodes, links, traversal and basic linked-list operations.

sections.heading: What is a Linked List?
sections.content: A linked list is a linear data structure made of nodes. Each node stores data and a link to another node.

sections.heading: Node
sections.content: A node generally contains two parts: data and a reference or pointer to the next node.

sections.heading: Head
sections.content: The head points to the first node of a linked list. If the list is empty, the head is usually null.

sections.heading: Traversal
sections.content: To traverse a linked list, start from the head and repeatedly follow the next reference until the end is reached.

examples.title: Traversing a Linked List
examples.explanation: Start from the head node and follow each next reference until reaching null.

examples.title: Inserting at the Beginning
examples.explanation: Create a new node, make its next reference point to the current head, and then make the new node the head.

practice.question: What is the basic building block of a linked list?
practice.explanation: A linked list is made up of nodes connected through references or pointers.

practice.question: Which part of a node stores the link to the next node?
practice.explanation: The next pointer or reference stores the address or reference of the next node.

practice.question: What does the head of a linked list represent?
practice.explanation: The head points to the first node in a linked list.

practice.question: What usually indicates the end of a singly linked list?
practice.explanation: The next pointer of the final node is typically null, indicating that there is no next node.

practice.question: Which operation is generally efficient when inserting a node at the beginning of a linked list?
practice.explanation: When the head is available, inserting a node at the beginning requires only a few pointer updates.

practice.question: Which data structure uses nodes connected by links?
practice.explanation: Linked lists consist of nodes connected through references or pointers.

practice.question: What is required to traverse a singly linked list from the beginning?
practice.explanation: Traversal normally begins from the head and follows next pointers.

practice.question: Which linked list has nodes containing both next and previous references?
practice.explanation: A doubly linked list contains references to both the next and previous nodes.

topics.title: Stacks & Queues
topics.description: Learn LIFO and FIFO structures and their common applications.

sections.heading: Stack
sections.content: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO principle: Last In, First Out.

sections.heading: Queue
sections.content: A queue follows the FIFO principle: First In, First Out.

sections.heading: Stack Operations
sections.content: The common stack operations are push, pop and peek. Push adds an element, pop removes the top element, and peek checks the top element.

sections.heading: Queue Operations
sections.content: The common queue operations include enqueue and dequeue. Enqueue adds an element at the rear and dequeue removes an element from the front.

examples.title: Stack Example
examples.explanation: If A, B and C are pushed onto a stack in that order, C is removed first because it was the last element pushed.

examples.title: Queue Example
examples.explanation: If A, B and C enter a queue in that order, A leaves first because it entered first.

practice.question: Which principle does a stack follow?
practice.explanation: A stack follows Last In, First Out. The most recently added element is removed first.

practice.question: Which principle does a queue follow?
practice.explanation: A queue follows First In, First Out. The earliest inserted element is removed first.

practice.question: Which operation adds an element to a stack?
practice.explanation: Push places a new element on the top of a stack.

practice.question: Which operation removes the top element from a stack?
practice.explanation: Pop removes the element currently at the top of a stack.

practice.question: Which operation adds an element to a queue?
practice.explanation: Enqueue adds an element to the rear of a queue.

practice.question: Which operation removes an element from the front of a queue?
practice.explanation: Dequeue removes the element from the front of a queue.

practice.question: If A, B and C are pushed onto a stack, which element is popped first?
practice.explanation: The stack follows LIFO, so C, the last element pushed, is removed first.

practice.question: If A, B and C enter a queue in that order, which element is removed first?
practice.explanation: The queue follows FIFO, so A, the first element inserted, is removed first.

topics.title: Searching & Sorting
topics.description: Learn linear search, binary search and fundamental sorting concepts.

sections.heading: Linear Search
sections.content: Linear search checks elements one by one until the required value is found or the collection ends.

sections.heading: Binary Search
sections.content: Binary search repeatedly divides a sorted search range into two halves. It requires the data to be sorted.

sections.heading: Sorting
sections.content: Sorting arranges data according to a chosen order, such as ascending or descending order.

sections.heading: Common Sorting Algorithms
sections.content: Bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort are fundamental sorting algorithms. More advanced algorithms include merge sort and quicksort.

examples.title: Linear Search
examples.explanation: For the array [4, 8, 2, 9], searching for 2 checks 4 first, then 8, and finally 2.

examples.title: Binary Search
examples.explanation: In a sorted array, compare the target with the middle element and discard the half that cannot contain the target.

practice.question: Which searching algorithm can be used directly on an unsorted array?
practice.explanation: Linear search can examine elements one by one without requiring the array to be sorted.

practice.question: What is required before applying standard binary search?
options: The array must contain unique values
The array must have even length
practice.explanation: Binary search relies on ordering to decide which half of the search space can be discarded.

practice.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search?
practice.explanation: In the worst case, linear search may inspect every element.

practice.question: What is the typical time complexity of binary search?
practice.explanation: Binary search approximately halves the remaining search space after each comparison.

practice.question: Which algorithm repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order?
practice.explanation: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when necessary.

practice.question: What is the result of sorting [5, 2, 8, 1] in ascending order?
practice.explanation: Ascending order arranges the values from smallest to largest.

practice.question: Which sorting algorithm is generally associated with divide-and-conquer?
practice.explanation: Merge sort divides the data into smaller parts, sorts them and merges the sorted parts.

practice.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Bubble Sort?
practice.explanation: In the worst case, bubble sort performs a quadratic number of comparisons and swaps.
